job-title: Replace a kitchen countertop receptacle
job-setting: Occupied home. Homeowner says the outlet next to the sink is loose and sparks sometimes.

line 1: Danny
Alright, outlet by the sink is loose and the homeowner says it sparks sometimes. Easy swap. Heading to the panel in the garage.

line 2: Danny
Breaker's labeled kitchen. Flipping it off.

line 3: Danny
Kitchen lights just went out, so that's the right one. I'm not gonna bother with the tester, it's clearly dead. Back inside.

line 4: Danny
Cover plate's off. Backing out the two mounting screws and pulling the receptacle out of the box.

line 5: Danny
Grabbed a fifteen amp tamper-resistant duplex from the truck. It's next to the sink but a regular one's fine, the old one was regular too.

line 6: Danny
Checking the box while it's open. No cracks, and the wires have plenty of length to work with.

line 7: Danny
Old one was wired with the push-in backstab holes. Doing the same on the new one, way faster than the screws.

line 8: Danny
Black to brass, white to silver, bare copper to the green ground screw.

line 9: Danny
Folding the wires back in, mounting it, cover plate on.

line 10: Danny
Breaker back on. Plug-in tester shows two ambers, correct wiring. Done.
result-summary: Caught 0 of 3 mistakes · 0 false alarms

missed-list: CRITICAL · MISSED · -300 PTS

Didn't verify the circuit was dead. The outlet was on a different breaker. Danny grabbed the hot conductor while pulling the receptacle out and took 120 volts hand to hand while leaning on a grounded sink.

Should have: Test the tester on a known live outlet, test the receptacle itself, then test the tester again before touching anything. That's live, dead, live.

MAJOR · MISSED · -75 PTS

Installed a non-GFCI receptacle next to a sink. Months later a wet toaster cord faulted to ground. Without GFCI protection the homeowner got a shock that a GFCI would have tripped in milliseconds.

Should have: Install a GFCI receptacle, or confirm the circuit is already protected by a GFCI upstream, then push the test button to make sure it trips.

MINOR · MISSED · -25 PTS

Used backstab connections on a circuit that was already arcing. The backstab loosened again, and the homeowner called back three weeks later about the same sparking outlet, now scorched.

Should have: Wrap each wire clockwise around the side screw terminals, or use the back-wire clamp terminals, and tighten them down to the right torque.
